cells.tense: You are drawing the form right now, and you know you are.
cells.ask: Put the whole structure on one page before you start building it, then build the first piece exactly that size.
cells.core:
There's a structure in front of you and you're the one drawing its lines. You start things in a form they can actually hold, and it's not fussiness — it's that you can see the shape before it exists and you build toward it without rushing the middle.

That's a rare thing. Most people start something and then try to find the frame for it later. You start with the frame. The work that comes from you carries its own pattern, which means other people can move inside it without guessing. Keep choosing from that clear place — not because it's tidy, but because nothing you care about gets built on a crooked line. The balance holds as long as you're choosing it, not just falling into it.
cells.sheetLine: You draw the frame before the walls go up.
cells.verb: Starting something in a form it can hold
cells.place: where the pattern gets set and the frame gets drawn

cells.tense: You are already building ahead of a shape that has not shown itself yet.
cells.ask: Pick one structure you've sketched out and leave it on the page for a week without adding a single line.
cells.core:
You can see structure where there isn't one yet, and you're laying it down before the thing has arrived. Plans for next season, systems that haven't been needed, frames built for people who haven't asked. Somewhere ahead is a version of all this where the shape is clear and you've already built for it.

The problem is that the thing itself hasn't had room to show you its form. You write the form in before it can be read. The structure starts answering for itself, and the meeting with what's actually here keeps getting postponed. Let one thing stay formless a little longer. The pattern can wait. What it's for won't wait forever, but it will wait a week.

cells.tense: You are standing behind a starting point that has already passed you by.
cells.ask: Finish one structure that's been sitting half-drawn — even badly, even small — and put it where you can see it done.
cells.core:
There's a form you can hold and you're not holding it. The impulse to organize is still in you. It just stays out of the open, so things around you sit loose — no pattern set, no frame drawn, no container built. Nothing gets closed, and whatever is loudest fills the space that structure would have held.

What's thin here isn't order or discipline. It's the sense that a structure you draw will be allowed to stand. The old one doesn't need repairing. One thing finished, small and visible, is enough to show the drawing hand that what it makes can hold. Pick the smallest unfinished thing and close it. Badly is fine. Done is the point.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped trusting the drawing hand, not the drawing.
cells.verb: Starting something in a form it can hold
cells.place: where the pattern gets set and the frame gets drawn

cells.tense: You are setting the pattern already, and you are calling it just how things run.
cells.ask: Name one routine you've set up around you as yours, out loud, and let it be a choice instead of a fact.
cells.core:
You're already arranging things — the flow of a morning, the order people move in, what gets decided and when. It shapes the days close to you, including yours. But if someone asked about it, you'd say that's just how it works here.

You set a pattern and then speak as though it arrived on its own. There's a simpler version underneath: you wanted something to hold, so you built a shape that holds it. The frame is yours and has been the whole time. Saying so takes nothing away. It puts you back in the room where the drawing happens.
cells.sheetLine: The pattern is yours. You've been calling it how things run.

attempts.check: The weakest claim in the draft was the Too Much cell saying the person is 'already living at the end' — the record gives bracing/writing-in-advance from Definition Bound, not arrival at the end, and a person mid-build would object that they're still at the beginning. The ask is still useful if the read is wrong (noticing what's missing from the structure is observable regardless of whether the bracing picture is right). The sentence that served me more than them was 'You're afraid the structure won't hold what you put in it' — it put a feeling in their mouth the record doesn't support; I cut it and stayed with the observable habit of building before the thing has shown its shape. The Too Little cell had to stay narrow enough that it doesn't locate a particular past room — 'somewhere you started a structure and the footing didn't hold' describes something they can recognize or refuse without being told what happened there.
